column1: What cognitive science principle, published by George Miller in 1956, defines the fundamental invariant governing slide information density?
column2: The 'magical number seven, plus or minus two'—the limit of concurrent information chunks (roughly 5-9) humans can hold in working memory at once.

column1: What is the first invariant of slide design regarding information optimization?
column2: Effective slides optimize for comprehension bandwidth rather than information volume, since presentations are linear in time with no audience-controlled rewind mechanism.

column1: What are the three layers of the visual information hierarchy that map to human perception pathways, and their time windows?
column2: 1) Pre-attentive processing (200-500ms): unconscious registration of color, size, position, motion. 2) Focal attention allocation: conscious gaze direction based on salience cues. 3) Sustained cognitive processing: semantic meaning extraction from text/data.

column1: Why do dense, uniform bullet-point slides fail according to the information density constraint?
column2: They collapse all information into the third (sustained cognitive processing) layer, forcing the brain to simultaneously parse many bullets, track the speaker's narrative, and integrate both streams—exceeding working memory capacity.

column1: What are the three core invariants of layout and typography design in PowerPoint?
column2: 1) Spatial consistency (reduces cognitive overhead via predictable element placement), 2) Typographic differentiation (scale/weight/color encode semantic meaning/hierarchy), 3) White space as intentional structural material (encodes priority through spatial generosity).

column1: What grid system do most default PowerPoint templates use, and what is its origin?
column2: A 12-column grid system at 960 pixels wide (for standard 10-inch slide width), borrowed directly from web design convention.

column1: Why does typographic contrast (e.g., 44pt heading vs 11pt body) work faster than reading comprehension?
column2: The human visual cortex recognizes pattern deviation (scale/weight contrast) in milliseconds, processing it pre-attentively—long before the prefrontal cortex reads and comprehends the actual words.

column1: What is PowerPoint's 'true function' according to Lesson 3, beyond being a document generation tool?
column2: PowerPoint is a narrative sequencing engine that controls information revelation across time, engineering a state-transition graph that moves audiences from their current mental model to a new one.

column1: What is the temporal binding constraint in presentation narrative design?
column2: Presentations impose a one-directional time stream controlled by the presenter (unlike documents with reader-controlled pacing), creating both a constraint (no random access to prior slides) and an opportunity (engineering anticipation and controlling cognitive load curve).

column1: Why does emotional scaffolding improve retention in business/technical presentations, per the neuroscience cited in Lesson 3?
column2: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex processes emotional significance and connects directly to memory consolidation systems, so information delivered without emotional context has measurably lower retention—logical frameworks embedded in narrative tension retain better.

column1: What is the required initial orientation phase duration when a new slide appears, and why must presenters delay speaking?
column2: 1.5 to 3 seconds; audiences need this window to construct a spatial map of content before processing semantic meaning. Speaking immediately creates a split-attention effect, forcing an impossible dual-channel decoding task (visual scanning + verbal narration).

column1: What is the optimal duration range for slide transitions, and what happens outside this range?
column2: 300-800 milliseconds, aligning with the psychological 'subjective present' where sensory events fuse into unified experience. Shorter durations cause disorienting flicker; longer than ~1 second become noticeable wait states disrupting narrative momentum.
